chapter_theme: Poems 221-240 are all laments (kaiyarunilai) for dead patrons: Pothiyar's three for Kopperunchozhan, whose friend was told to follow later and who as a hero-stone still makes room for old friends; laments for Karikalan, Nalankilli and Killi Valavan that reproach Death as a fool who ate its own seed or a suppliant who had to beg; the potter asked for an urn as big as the earth; Avvai's laments for Anji, his pyre, his hero-stone and the toddy he shared; poems for Evvi, Pari, Ilaveliman, Nambi Nedunchezhiyan and Aay, ending in the bard's resolve to seek a new patron and the scattering of poets to other lands.

221.reading: The poet lists what the dead king was: fame given to singers, love given to dancers, a just sceptre praised by the virtuous, firm friendship praised by the able, gentleness to women and strength to men, a home for the learned; Death, which does not weigh such worth, took his life, so he calls the truthful poets to come, hold the grieving kin, and revile Death, saying the patron has become a hero-stone wearing unfading fame while the wide world hangs in sorrow.
221.nuance: The catalogue of six balanced half-lines is undone by one word, நினையாக் கூற்றம்: Death is blamed not for cruelty but for not thinking, for failing to weigh the very qualities the poem has just counted. The patron's end is a stone that wears fame like a garland (சூடி).

thinai_evidence.note: it laments a patron taken by Death and turned into a hero-stone, the matter of kaanchi's kaiyarunilai (porul 2.19)

222.reading: Speaking to the dead king, the poet recalls that he was told to come only after the famous son had been born to the king's wife, she who wears flame-bright jewels and never leaves him even as his shadow, and so was left behind here; he calls the king loveless and asks what place he now has, since the king, a lover of fame, is not one to sit without thinking of him.
222.nuance: The poem does not name what the king was doing or what 'come' meant; read with 223 and the colophon's patron, the summons is to join him in his chosen death, so 'loveless' is a friend's reproach for being kept from dying with him, and the son's birth is the duty that held the poet back.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend left behind by a dead king laments his own exclusion, a kaanchi kaiyarunilai

comparisons.tenor: the wife's constancy to the king
the brightness of her jewels

223.reading: Having been shade to many and praised high by the world, the king, unable to go on, folded into a narrow place; yet even now that he has become an enduring hero-stone, he surely gives room and welcome to the old friends of long intimacy, whose bond is as close as life's love for the body, if they go to him.
223.nuance: The hospitality the king showed alive (இடங் கொடுத்து அளிப்ப) is credited to the stone, so the friends who follow him in death are pictured as guests arriving at his gate; line 2 (தலைப்போ கன்மையிற் சிறுவழி மடங்கி) is compressed and may describe his last confinement rather than the stone's narrow site.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a king become a hero-stone and turns on the old friends who go to join him

comparisons.tenor: the king as protector of many
the closeness of old friends to the king

224.reading: The poet recounts the dead king's deeds: he overran battle without regard for forts, drank jars of toddy with his companions and kept the bards' large families, and in an assembly that knew right order completed the Vedic sacrifice with its sun-shaped layered altar and tall post, with his wives of spotless conduct; such a wise man is dead, and the world is to be pitied, for his gentle women have stripped off their ornaments like a vengai tree that cowherds have lopped bare, flowers and all, to feed their hungry herd in a summer of failed falls and great drought.
224.nuance: The three -ததூஉம் clauses (fighting, feeding, sacrificing) build a sentence that never reaches a main verb of praise; it breaks into இறந்தோன் தானே. The closing simile is cruelly exact: the vengai is stripped not by malice but by need, as the women strip their jewels because the custom of widowhood demands it.

thinai_evidence.note: it lists a dead king's deeds and ends on his widows' stripped ornaments, the grief of kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the circular layered enclosure of the sacrificial altar
the widows who have removed their ornaments

225.reading: The poet describes the king's army so long that its van ate sweet palmyra pulp while its middle ate ripe fruit and its rear roasted tubers, an army that circled the earth and broke kings' pride, and says that this strength is now to be seen in the thorny waste where kalli grows, the cremation ground; he grieves that the twisted valampuri conch, once proclaiming victory with the drums and now hung to one side like a weaver bird's hanging nest, may sound at dawn at the gates of other kings.
225.nuance: The army is measured by what its three parts eat at the same moment, so its length is a span of the land's foods. Lines 13 and 14 are hard: the grief may be that the dead king's conch, now hung aside, will be blown at other kings' gates, his emblem passing to new masters.

thinai_evidence.note: it sets a conqueror's army against the cremation ground where he now lies, kaanchi's world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: the king's conch hung up on one side

226.reading: Whether it raged, burned with anger or fought, Death could not have escaped Valavan; to take the king of the golden garland, the strong chariot and the army that crosses fierce battle, it must have begged him, joining its hands and praising him as the singers do.
226.nuance: The praise is double: no force could take him, and no request was ever refused by him, so Death succeeded only by joining the bards. The king's generosity becomes the cause of his death.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a king's death by making Death a suppliant, a kaanchi poem on inescapable Death turned inside out

comparisons.tenor: Death approaching the king

227.reading: The poet calls Death a fool without sense, which for want of skill has cooked and eaten its own seed: Valavan, whose bee-swarmed garland and golden ornaments matched Death's own strength, fed Death's hunger every day by conquering and killing warriors, elephants and horses on fields flooded with blood; having taken such a man, who will now relieve its hunger?
227.nuance: The mockery is a form of grief: by calling Death stupid, the poet keeps the king's killing power at the centre, and the threat in line 3 (you will yet see whether I speak true) is that Death will now go hungry.

thinai_evidence.note: it reproaches Death for taking a king, the grief of kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: Death's killing of the king who supplied it with victims
Valavan, a killer equal to Death

228.reading: The poet calls on the potter of the old wide town, whose kiln plants in the sky a smoke as thick as darkness, and pities him: Valavan, descendant of the Chembiyans, whose army crowned the earth and whose fame shone far like the sun climbing the sky, has reached the world of the gods, and if the potter means to make an urn wide enough to cover him, he would need the great earth for his wheel and a great mountain for his clay.
228.nuance: Grief is spoken as a practical problem set to a craftsman: the poet never weeps, he only shows that no urn could be large enough, and the triple call to the potter (lines 1 and 4) is the lament's refrain.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a dead king through the urn that must hold him, a kaanchi lament

comparisons.tenor: the kiln's smoke
the king's far-shining eminence
the size of urn the king's greatness demands

229.reading: The poet records that on a Panguni midnight, when certain stars stood in their places, a star fell from the sky blazing like a lamp for the sea-girt land; seeing it, he and many other suppliants feared for the lord of the good land of drum-loud falls, and on the seventh day, with his elephant asleep with its trunk laid down, his drum rolling with its face torn, his white umbrella broken and his horse standing still, the king went to the upper world; the poet asks whether, now a support to bright-bangled women there, he has forgotten his own companions, he who bound his foes and gave without measure, dark like a sapphire mountain.
229.nuance: The opening twelve lines fix the night by asterisms (lines 1 to 8), which this reading cannot identify with confidence; what is clear is that the omen comes first and the death seven days later, and that the royal emblems (elephant, drum, umbrella, horse) fail before he dies. The closing question imagines him in heaven, a support to women there, as if he had simply moved patrons.

thinai_evidence.note: an omen foretells a king's death and the poem mourns it, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the king's dark body
the falling star's blaze

230.reading: While Ezhini lived, herds stayed in the forest, travellers camped where they liked and grain heaps lay unguarded; now that the unfailing Ezhini of the unwavering sceptre and famed sword has fallen in battle, his kin grieve everywhere like a baby left by its mother and the world suffers in hunger, yet the poet tells unjust Death that it has lost more than they: like a farmer of a failing house who eats his seed grain not knowing the harvest it would bring, Death has eaten one man's life when, had it spared him, it could have drunk many enemies' lives on his battlefield.
230.nuance: The first three lines describe peace by things left unguarded, so the king's protection is shown as an absence of fear. The argument against Death is an economic one: the loss of the protector is counted first as the people's loss and then, as a bitter joke, as Death's.

thinai_evidence.note: it laments a chieftain fallen in battle and reproaches Death, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the dead chieftain's kin
Death eating Ezhini's life

231.reading: Let the bright flame of the pyre, of charred wood like the half-burnt logs of a hill farmer's burnt field, shrink low, or let it not shrink but rise till it touches the sky: the fame of the man who was like the bright sun, with a white umbrella like the cool-rayed moon, will not perish.
231.nuance: Avvai concedes everything about the pyre (let it be small, let it be huge) to deny it the one thing that matters; the sun and moon of the last lines are what fire cannot reach. குருகினும் in line 3 is unclear (smaller than a heron, or than a smith's bellows); the sense of shrinking is not in doubt.

thinai_evidence.note: it sets the funeral pyre against undying fame, kaanchi's world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: the charred wood of the pyre
the king's white umbrella
the dead king

232.reading: Let there be no more mornings and evenings, and no more days of my life: will he who would not accept even a country of high-peaked mountains given to him now accept the toddy, strained through fibre, poured from a small cup on his hero-stone crowned with a peacock feather?
232.nuance: The question turns on accepting (கொள்வன் கொல்): the man famous for refusing even a whole country as a gift is now offered a small cup, so the hero-stone rite is felt as an insult to his greatness and the poet's grief takes the form of disbelief.

thinai_evidence.note: it laments a dead patron before his hero-stone, kaanchi

233.reading: Let it be false, let it be false, as false as the golden wheel that was said to appear with Akuthai, who never lacked elephants to give to suppliants: the voice that at dawn announced that Evvi, leader of the bards' great families, of great ornaments and a battle-killing army, had many deep spear wounds in his chest.
233.nuance: The poem is all denial: the death itself is never stated, only the report of the wounds, which the poet wishes into a famous falsehood. What the story of Akuthai's golden wheel was cannot be recovered from the poem; it serves here as a proverbially false report.

thinai_evidence.note: it refuses the news of a patron's mortal wounds, a kaanchi lament

comparisons.tenor: the dawn report of Evvi's wounds

234.reading: Shall I grieve? Let the mornings wane: how did he eat the small sweet ball of rice that his beloved wife set on grass, on a small spot she smeared clean no bigger than a she-elephant's footprint, he who was used to eating with many at a gate opened for the whole world to enter?
234.nuance: Everything in the rite is small (சிறுவழி, இன்சிறு பிண்டம்) against the wide gate of his life, and the grief is that the host who never ate alone is now fed alone, by one hand.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a dead patron through the funeral offering set for him, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the small cleaned spot for the offering

235.reading: Avvai remembers how Anji gave her any little toddy he got and drank the larger share happily while she sang, shared his rice in many dishes whether it was little or much, gave her every bone with meat on it and stood himself wherever arrow and spear went in, and stroked her flesh-smelling head with his narantham-scented hand; the spear that pierced his chest went through the bowls of the bards and the hands of suppliants, dimmed the eyes of those he kept, and fell on the tongues of poets; now there is no one to sing and no one to give to singers, and many lives die giving nothing, like the fragrant pakanrai flowers of the cold ford that wither unworn.
235.nuance: The repeated மன்னே ('it was so, once') turns each memory into a loss as it is spoken. The spear is followed through everyone who lived off Anji, so one wound becomes the wound of a whole economy of giving; the last lines turn from him to the rest, who die like flowers no one wore.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a patron killed by a spear and remembers his giving, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the death of Anji striking all who depended on him
lives that end without giving

236.reading: Addressing Pari, lord of the hill land where the great jackfruit, like a drum, torn open by the stag's feeding becomes the hunters' food, Kapilar says that he was not true to their close friendship: he must have been angry with him, for in the years he kept him, against the honour of their friendship, he would not let him come with him and said 'stay behind', and so Kapilar is not with him; still, may high fate, which showed them this life together, grant him in the next life to live with Pari without parting.
236.nuance: The opening image of plenty (the stag's leftover fruit feeding the hunters) is Pari's hill as it was; the reproach that follows is the same as Pothiyar's in 222, that the patron forbade his friend to follow him, and Kapilar answers it not by dying but by asking fate for the next birth.

thinai_evidence.note: a friend mourns a dead patron and asks to rejoin him in the next birth, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the great jackfruit

237.reading: On his day of hunger the poet came to the patron's tall gate singing 'long may you live', trusting that the verse he had sown in the ear of that unfailing man, rich shade in a hot season, had ripened; that hope came to nothing, as if the cooking pot had yielded only fire, for unjust Death, never saying 'let these poor people eat', struck without reason, and amid widows scattering their broken bangles like plantain-flower petals and grieving old kin and gift-seekers, the young white-speared hero went to the kalli-grown cremation ground and perished; yet let that be no sorrow: a tiger that misses the elephant it stalked will not stalk a rat, so he bids his heart rise with resolve and rush like a river into the sea to bring great gifts.
237.nuance: The poem moves from kaiyarunilai to a bard's resolve: grief is set aside by the tiger proverb, which makes the poet's pride (only a great patron will do) the reason to stop mourning. The cremation line (13) is the same as 225 line 7.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a patron's death and turns to the bard's next journey, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the patron as protector of the hungry
the poet's hope that his song will be rewarded
the hope that yielded only ruin
the widows' broken bangles
the poet who will seek only a great patron
the poet's going to a new patron

238.reading: He who loved toddy has gone ahead to the cremation forest, where on the round back of an overturned red urn the red-eared cock and the pokuval, unafraid, and the hard-beaked crow and the owl gather and roam at will with troops of ghosts; the bards' families have wilted, their old beauty gone like women who have taken off their bangles, the strapped drums have their faces torn, the riderless mountain-like elephants have lost their tusks; since fierce Death has struck, the poet, who came not knowing his lord had fallen, asks what will become of those who depend on him, and, his heart in anguish, whirling like a blind mute fallen into the sea on a rainy night when trees come down, says that to perish would be best and fitting.
238.nuance: The poet arrives too late, and the poem's horror is placed in the birds who are no longer afraid; the blind mute in the sea is a man who can neither see a way nor call for help. Line 11 (ஆகுல அதற்படல்) is corrupt or obscure, and the reading of it as his not knowing of the death is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a patron gone to the cremation ground and ends wishing for death, kaanchi

karu.sense: a bird of the burning ground

comparisons.tenor: the wilted families of the bards
the elephants
the poet in his grief

239.reading: The poet lists all the dead man did: he embraced bangled women, wore flowers from guarded groves, smeared cool fragrant sandal, destroyed his foes' line, raised his friends, did not fawn on the strong or lord it over the weak, never begged and never refused a beggar, won fame in kings' assemblies, held off advancing armies and saw retreating ones turn their backs, rode swift horses, drove chariots down long streets, rode tall elephants, drained jars of sweet toddy, ended the bards' hunger to their joy, and gave up confusing speech; since he did everything that should be done, let them bury him or burn him, wherever this lover of fame's head may fall.
239.nuance: Pleasures (women, flowers, sandal, toddy) stand in the same list as justice, courage and giving, with no ranking between them: a complete life is a full life, and because it was complete the body's fate does not matter, a defiant answer to the funeral rite itself.

thinai_evidence.note: a full life is counted at its end and the manner of disposal is left indifferent, kaanchi

240.reading: Aay Andiran, who never stinted singers of dancing-gaited horses, elephants, chariots, and lands and towns of unfailing yield, has been carried off with his women of small bangles by the eyeless one called Kaalan to the upper world; resting on one side of the kalli-grown waste where the split-beaked owl in its hollow calls to the dead 'burn and heap', his body was consumed by the bright fire, and now the poets, eyes dimmed, not seeing their patron, helpless with their clamouring kin and wasted with hunger, have become travellers to other men's lands.
240.nuance: Line 4 sends his women with him to the upper world, so the poem records wives dying with the chief. The last image is the social consequence of a patron's death: his poets become migrants, the opposite of the fixed bounty listed in lines 1 to 3.

thinai_evidence.note: it mourns a patron's cremation and the scattering of his poets, kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: Death, which takes without seeing whom

links.note: Kural 771 boasts that many who stood against the speaker's lord now stand as stones (கல்நின் றவர்); 221 ends with the generous patron himself become a hero-stone (நடுகல் ஆயினன் புரவலன்), mourned by poets.
links.teaches: In the Kural the hero-stone is the fate a warrior threatens on his enemies, while in 221 it is the end of the patron the poets loved, so the same stone that marks a foe's defeat also marks the giver's fame, and the boast of 771 is one side of a monument that kaiyarunilai shows from the other.

links.note: Akananuru 55 recalls Cheralathan sitting facing north (வான்வடக் கிருந்தென) after his wound at Venni and the worthies who went with him to the other world; in 222 the poet reproaches his king for telling him to come only after his son was born.
links.teaches: The akam simile shows that companions dying with a king who sat facing north was a known and honoured act, which explains why being told to wait for a son's birth is felt in 222 as a lack of love: the friend was barred from an honour the custom gave him.

links.note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as a bond that never curtails the liberties of intimacy (கிழமை); 223 says the king, even as a hero-stone, gives room to friends of old intimacy (கிழமைத் தொன்னட் புடையார்) who come to him.
links.teaches: The Kural's definition is carried past death in 223: the claim of intimacy that a friend may exercise unasked includes the right to follow the king into death, and the stone honours it by making room, so pazhaimai is tested at its extreme.

links.note: 224 mourns the king of the colophon, Karikalan, listing his battles, feeding of bards and sacrifice; Akananuru 55 recalls Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni, after which the defeated Cheral sat facing north and worthies died with him.
links.teaches: Karikalan is remembered in the akam simile through the mourning his victory caused in the defeated court, and in 224 through his own women's stripped ornaments, so the same king stands in the corpus at both ends of the grief that war produces.

links.note: Line 7 of 225 and line 13 of 237 are the same line, கள்ளி போகிய களரியம் பறந்தலை, naming the cremation ground where Nalankilli's strength now lies and where the young hero perished.
links.teaches: Two poets mourning different patrons reach for the identical line for the burning ground, which shows that kaiyarunilai drew on a shared stock of formulas, and that what made each poem particular was what it set on that ground: an army's might in 225, a bard's lost hope in 237.

links.note: Naladiyar 20 pictures merciless Death roaming for its victims and seizing even the unborn while the mother wails; 226 says Death could not have taken Valavan by rage or force and must have begged him like a bard.
links.teaches: On the Naladiyar's account no one escapes a Death that takes by force, while 226 claims that this king was beyond Death's force and fell only to his own generosity, so the bardic lament denies the very powerlessness before Death that the moralist uses to urge virtue.

links.note: 228 asks how a potter could make an urn big enough for Valavan, with the earth for his wheel and a mountain for clay; 231 says that whether Anji's pyre is low or reaches the sky, his fame will not perish.
links.teaches: 228 measures the king's greatness by the size of the funeral vessel it would need, while 231 declares the size of the pyre irrelevant to fame, so the two poems show the funeral rite being used both as the measure of greatness and as the thing greatness escapes.

links.note: 227 tells Death it has cooked and eaten its seed (வித்துஅட்டு உண்டனை) in taking Valavan; 230 likens Death to a failing farmer who eats his seed (வித்து உண்டாஅங்கு) in taking Ezhini.
links.teaches: Two poets on different kings make the same argument through the seed image, that a slain warrior was the source of Death's future harvest of enemies, which shows that taunting Death with its own loss was a recognised move in kaiyarunilai and not one poet's conceit.

links.note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except unmatched renown; 231 says Anji's fame will not perish whether his pyre shrinks or rises to the sky.
links.teaches: Avvai's poem gives the Kural's general claim its occasion: fame is undying precisely at the pyre, where everything else of the man is being burned, so the maxim's 'nothing else stands' is shown in the act of the body's ending.

links.note: In 235 Avvai remembers Anji sharing his toddy with her; in 232 she pictures toddy poured from a small cup on his hero-stone and asks whether he who refused a whole country will accept it.
links.teaches: The toddy he once shared with his poet returns in 232 as a funeral offering to his stone, so the rite reverses their old roles (now she gives and he must receive), which is why Avvai cannot believe he will accept it.

links.note: 233 refuses the dawn report of spear wounds on the chest of Evvi, leader of the bards' families; Akananuru 115 uses the bards who, in the battle where Evvi fell (எவ்வி வீழ்ந்த செருவில் பாணர்), broke off the curved necks of their lutes, as a simile for konrai pods on a desert path.
links.teaches: The akam poet assumes his hearers know that bards mourned Evvi by breaking their lutes, so the death the puram poet cannot bring himself to believe became, in the akam tradition, a fixed public memory usable as a passing image of curved pods.

links.note: Kural 229 says eating alone to fill one's own store is more bitter than begging; 234 grieves that Evvi, who always ate with many at a gate open to the world, is now fed alone a small rice ball on grass by his wife.
links.teaches: The Kural condemns solitary eating as the miser's choice, and 234 shows death forcing that very condition on the most open-handed host, so the bitterness the Kural assigns to the hoarder becomes, in the lament, the injury done to the giver by his funeral rite.

links.note: Kural 1007 likens the wealth of one who gives nothing to a beautiful woman growing old alone; 235 ends by likening the many lives that die without giving to pakanrai flowers that wither unworn.
links.teaches: Both books picture what is not given as beauty that no one enjoys, but Avvai moves the image from the miser's wealth to the miser's life and sets it against a giver who has just died, so the waste is measured by the loss of one who did give.

links.note: Kapilar says Pari told him 'stay behind' (ஒழிக) and would not let him come; Pothiyar says the king left him here (என்இவண் ஒழித்த) telling him to come only after his son's birth.
links.teaches: Two poets of different patrons voice the same grievance, that the patron forbade his friend to follow him in death, and Kapilar resolves it differently, by asking fate for the next birth, so the pair shows that kaiyarunilai had a recognised place for the friend refused the right to die with his lord.

links.note: Kural 772 says carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than an arrow that hit a hare; 237 says a tiger that misses the elephant it stalked will not stalk a rat, and the poet resolves to seek great gifts.
links.teaches: The Kural's warrior maxim about aiming high is used in 237 by a bard to turn from mourning to his next patron, so the ethic of the great target governed the bard's choice of patron as well as the soldier's choice of foe.

links.note: Kural 922 says not to drink toddy, and that only those who do not care to be counted by the worthy should; 239 lists draining jars of sweet toddy among the deeds of a man who 'did all that should be done' and so earned fame.
links.teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree about whether drinking belongs to a praiseworthy life: the Kural excludes the drinker from the esteem of the worthy, while the Purananuru lament counts the toddy jar beside justice and giving in a life complete enough to make the manner of burial indifferent.

links.note: 240 calls Aay Andiran never stinting singers of horses, elephants and chariots; Akananuru 152 names 'Aay's forest' after the Aay who gives elephants to all who come, skilled or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்).
links.teaches: The akam poet uses Aay's open-handedness to name a place, while the puram poem records what followed his death, his poets scattering to other lands, so the patron's giving outlived him as a landmark in love poetry even as the household it fed dissolved.

new_concepts.gloss: helplessness in grief: the lament of bards, friends or kin left without their patron or lord after his death, a thurai of kaanchi (porul 2.19) and the colophons' pothuviyal
new_concepts.label_source: The colophons of Purananuru 221 to 240 name it (கையறுநிலை), and 240 line 12 has கையழிந்து.

new_concepts.gloss: sitting facing north to die by fasting, the death a defeated or grieving king chose, which close friends might share
new_concepts.label_source: Akananuru 55 line 12 names it (வான்வடக் கிருந்தென); Purananuru 222 and 223 presuppose it in the friend told to come later and the friends who go to the stone.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard or poet receives from a patron, and the seeking of it
new_concepts.label_source: Purananuru 237 line 19 (பரிசில் தருகம்) and 233 line 2 (பரிசிலர்) use the word.

new_concepts.gloss: the hero-stone set up for a dead warrior or patron, crowned and given offerings, in which he is thought to abide
new_concepts.label_source: Purananuru 221 line 13, 223 line 3 and 232 line 3 use the word.

source_issues: 221 line 8: உய்த்த்ன்று is a misprint for உய்த்தன்று.
224 line 4: கணட is a misprint for கண்ட.
225 line 1: தீங்சோறு is a misprint for தீஞ்சோறு.
228 line 1: கலங்செய் (second time) is a misprint for கலஞ்செய்; line 13: அயின் is a misprint for ஆயின்.
